title: Curtailment Is Written Against Dates: Preparing FHA and Mortgage Insurance Claims With an AI Agent in Post-Default Servicing
summary: By the time a defaulted loan reaches the claim, every mistake made since the first missed payment shows up as a number someone deducts. A claim package is hundreds of pages of servicing history, invoices and legal fees that have to agree with each other, and FHA's curtailment rules punish the dates that do not. What we learned running a claims agent in production for a post-default claims outsourcer, where it helps, and why a specialist still files.
body_markdown:
## Who This Is For


Heads of Default Servicing, claims managers at servicers and at the outsourcers who prepare claims for them, and servicing compliance officers who sign off on what goes to HUD, VA and the mortgage insurers.


## The Last Desk Pays for Every Earlier Mistake


Every servicing leader knows the claim is where default losses get decided, and most of them treat it as a back-office function. That is a mistake I understand, because the claim desk sits at the very end of a long process. A loan goes delinquent, loss mitigation runs and fails, the loan is referred to foreclosure, the sale happens, the property is secured and maintained and eventually conveyed or sold, and only then does someone sit down to ask the insurer or guarantor for the money. By then, everything that happened over eighteen months or three years is fixed in the record. The claim specialist cannot change any of it. They can only add it up correctly, and find what the record will cost.


What it costs is usually a curtailment. The insurer pays less than the claim because a deadline was missed, an expense was not allowable, an invoice exceeded a limit without approval, or the dates in the file do not support the interest being claimed. Some curtailments are fair. Many are avoidable, because the evidence that would have defended the date or the expense was in the file and nobody found it before the claim went out.


## What a Claim Package Actually Is


People outside default servicing tend to picture a claim as a form. It is a reconciliation. For an FHA conveyance claim, the servicer files form HUD-27011, the Single Family Application for Insurance Benefits, through FHA Connection, and the numbers on it have to be supported by the servicing history, the corporate advance ledger, the escrow disbursements for taxes and insurance, the foreclosure attorney's invoices, the property preservation vendor's work orders and photos, the bankruptcy record if there was one, the loss mitigation history, and the title and deed documents for the conveyance. On a typical file that is hundreds of pages from a dozen sources, most of which were never designed to agree with each other.


A specialist preparing that claim spends most of their time reading and cross-checking, not entering numbers. Does the date the foreclosure attorney says the first legal action was filed match the court record? Was the grass-cutting invoice for a date after the property was vacant, and is it within the allowable? Is the hazard insurance disbursement in the ledger the same premium as the declaration page? Each of those checks is small, and there are hundreds of them per claim.


## Curtailment Is Written Against Dates


FHA's rules make dates the main battleground. Under[24 CFR 203.356](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/section-203.356) , the mortgagee has to pursue foreclosure with reasonable diligence within HUD's timeframes, and[24 CFR 203.402](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-24/section-203.402) provides for curtailing debenture interest when those timeframes, or HUD's reporting requirements, are not met. HUD's own mortgagee letters have warned for decades that debenture interest curtailments can cost a mortgagee a lot of money, and the arithmetic agrees: interest on a large unpaid balance, cut back months to the date the foreclosure should have finished, adds up fast.


Two details make this harder than it sounds. First, the servicer curtails itself. The mortgagee identifies its own interest curtailment date on the HUD-27011 when it files, and if it later finds it under-curtailed, it remits the difference to HUD through FHA Connection's claim remittance function. Second, the timeframe clock can be extended for reasons beyond the servicer's control, such as a bankruptcy filing, a state-mandated mediation, or a loss mitigation review that paused the foreclosure, but only if the file documents the delay. A servicer that cannot evidence the bankruptcy stay dates or the mediation period will self-curtail more interest than it had to, and one that claims the extension without the evidence has certified a number it cannot support.


That second case is the one compliance should worry about. A claim submitted to HUD is a claim for federal funds, and an incorrect certification is the kind of thing the[False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. 3729](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/31/3729) , was written for. Getting the curtailment date right in both directions is a financial question and a compliance question at the same time.


Private mortgage insurance works on a similar logic under each insurer's master policy, which sets its own deadlines for notices of default, for filing the claim after the sale, and for which expenses are covered. VA guaranty claims go through VALERI with VA's own rules about allowable fees and timelines. Each of these goes into the[Rulebook](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#rulebook) as a separate rule set, because the same loan event can be on time for one payer and late for another.


## What We Built, and Where It Runs


The[Claims Analyst](https://www.seiright.com/for-servicers/claims-analyst) desk in UMOS runs in production today for a post-default claims outsourcer, a firm whose business is preparing claims on behalf of servicers. That setting tests an agent quickly, because files arrive in whatever format, ledger layout and vendor invoice style each servicer uses, and none of them match.


The agent ingests the whole package behind a claim: servicing history, disbursement ledgers, legal invoices, property preservation records, and everything else the servicer sends. It extracts the fields the claim form needs and, more usefully, reconciles them against each other. The first legal action date from the attorney's invoice is compared with the date on the filed complaint or notice of sale. The sale date is compared across the attorney's records, the deed, and the servicing notes. Every expense in the ledger is matched to an invoice, and every invoice to the line it supports. Where two sources disagree, the agent flags the disagreement with both pages side by side.


It then presents the result as a structured view a specialist can verify at a glance: each claim line, its amount, its source documents and any flag, with the dates and amounts most likely to draw a curtailment marked before the claim is filed. We built it that way because a list of extracted fields saves a specialist almost nothing: they would still have to re-check every one. A view where everything that agrees is cited and marked as agreeing lets them spend their attention on the handful of lines that do not.


## Why the Specialist Files, Not the Agent


We made a firm decision that the agent never files a claim. A specialist reviews and files, and anything the agent cannot reconcile reaches them as a named exception beside the page it came from. There are three reasons.


The first is the certification. Someone at the servicer is attesting to HUD or to an insurer that the claim is correct, and that person should have looked at it. The second is judgment on contested items. Whether a delay was really outside the servicer's control, or whether an expense that exceeded an allowable was reasonable enough to request approval for, are calls where an experienced specialist adds something an agent should not decide alone. The third is accountability to the client. An outsourcer's clients want to know a person they can name stands behind the claim, and that is a reasonable thing to want.


Everything the agent does is in the[Evidence Trail](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#evidence-trail) , cited to the document and page, so when an insurer questions a line six months later, the answer to "where did this number come from" is already written down. That matters more in claims than almost anywhere else in servicing, because claims get audited long after the people who prepared them have moved on.


## Fixing It Upstream


The most useful thing a claims agent does may be what it tells the rest of the servicing operation. When the same kind of curtailment shows up across dozens of claims, such as a foreclosure step that keeps running past its timeframe in one state, or property preservation invoices that keep exceeding allowables with one vendor, the cause sits in the default process months earlier, and the claim is only where it gets priced. On the servicer side, the[Default Management Desk](https://www.seiright.com/for-servicers/default-management-desk) tracks every investor and insurer milestone so the date that would become a curtailment is flagged before it slips, and the claims findings are what tell you which milestones to watch hardest.


That is also where the[government loan waterfall changes](https://www.seiright.com/blog/government-loan-default-servicing-fha-va-loss-mitigation-waterfall-ai) matter: a loss mitigation option offered or skipped in year one becomes a timeline question at the claim in year three. When the claim desk and the default desk read the same[Loan Graph](https://www.seiright.com/platform/loan-graph) , the loss gets cheaper because the dates got defended while they could still be met.


If you run a claims operation, pull your last quarter's curtailments by reason code. My guess is that most of the dollars sit in a small number of reasons, and most of those reasons were visible in the file before the claim was filed. That is the work an agent should take on first.
